title: How to Decide Which Products Deserve a Subscribe-and-Save Option
excerpt: A four-part filter for choosing which SKUs earn a subscription option: consumption rhythm, margin headroom after discount, shipping behavior, and the support load you take on.
body: Adding subscribe-and-save to every product looks like a growth lever and behaves like a margin leak. Subscription only works when the customer's consumption is predictable, the product ships without drama, and the discount you give away is smaller than the retention you buy. Before you install anything, run your catalog through a filter. The DTCwise Subscription & Loyalty category at /category/subscription keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing for teams at exactly this decision.

The first test is consumption rhythm. Ask a simple question: does a customer finish this product and need another one inside a window they can name? Coffee, supplements, skincare refills, pet supplies, and filters pass easily. Apparel, seasonal decor, and anything bought as a gift fail immediately. If the honest answer is that some customers reorder and some do not, split the difference and offer a subscription only on the size or bundle that repeat buyers actually choose, rather than on every variant in the listing.

The second test is margin headroom after the discount. Take contribution margin, subtract the subscription discount, subtract the extra shipping you will absorb on smaller repeat orders, and look at what is left. A fifteen percent discount on a product with sixty percent margin is a reasonable trade for a predictable second and third order. The same fifteen percent on a thirty-five percent margin product turns a good customer into a break-even one. Run this per SKU on a spreadsheet before you promise anything publicly.

The third test is shipping behavior. Subscription orders tend to be smaller than one-time orders, which pushes shipping cost per order up and makes your free-shipping threshold behave differently. Check whether the subscription SKU can ride along in a box that already ships profitably, and whether the cadence you offer lines up with a basket size worth shipping. Weekly cadence on a low-priced item is usually a shipping problem wearing a convenience feature as a costume.

The fourth test is support load. Every recurring order is a chance for something to go wrong: a card expires, a customer wants to skip a month, a shipment arrives late. If support is one person answering email, start with a narrow offer on two or three SKUs plus a clear self-serve skip and pause control. Check /tool/recharge on DTCwise when comparing how billing apps handle dunning and self-serve changes, because that is where the support load actually lands.

Roll out in three waves instead of all at once. Wave one is your highest-repeat SKU with the clearest cadence. Wave two adds the bundle or the larger size. Wave three is whatever survived two months of real data. At each wave, watch three numbers: second-order rate, average subscription lifespan in months, and support tickets per hundred subscribers. If lifespan sits under three months, the product is not a subscription product and your discount is just a permanent price cut. The DTCwise Subscription & Loyalty category at /category/subscription keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing, so you can compare options before the next wave.
